newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait's KIA says taxation could hamper reform.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait's KIA says taxation could hamper reform.

text.p: Kuwait's economic reform would be negatively affected by any imposition of taxes, the Director General of the Kuwait Investment Authority (KIA) said in remarks published on Tuesday.
"It is not in the interest of the economic reform plan to have taxes now," al-Qabas newspaper quoted Ali al-Badr as saying.
"After a certain period, when the community accepts the idea of economic reform, the state could resort to imposing selective taxes or finance-oriented taxes upon need," he added.
MPs say Kuwaitis, long-used to generouse welfare benefits, reject taxation.
Kuwait imposes no local companies or on individual income. Only foreign firms operating in Kuwait pay tax on profits.
The oil-rich Gulf Arab state is trying to balance its books Its budget shortfalls were worsened by the huge costs of the 1991 Gulf War that ended a seven-month Iraqi occupation.
The government wants to eliminate the shortfall in the year 2000. It projects a 1.2 billion dinars ($4.0 billion) deficit on a 4.2 billion spending for the 1996/97 fiscal year (July-June).
A reform plan designed to achieve that target includes a wide-ranging privatisation programme, state spending cuts and increase of revenue from non-oil functions.
"We in Kuwait do not need taxes for financing (state expenditure) but we might need selective taxes, specifically on cigarettes and luxury goods," said Badr.
Kuwait, with a population of 2.0 million people of which 720,000 are nationals, sits on one tenth of the world's proven oil reserves and produces some 2.0 million barrels per day of oil.
